imgs.a: Organ of Corti in the cochlea

ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The cochlea is a spiral, fluid‑filled organ in the inner ear that converts sound vibrations into neural signals. Its precise architecture and blood supply are essential for hearing, and disruption leads to sensorineural hearing loss.

sections.p: The cochlea is a tapered, snail‑shaped structure in the petrous part of the temporal bone. It contains three fluid‑filled scalae and the organ of Corti, where mechanotransduction occurs.
b: Spiral shape ~2.5 turns
Contains scala vestibuli, media, and tympani
Organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane

sections.p: Located medial to the vestibule, the cochlea occupies the medial wall of the inner ear. Its bony labyrinth houses the membranous labyrinth, which includes the scalae and the cochlear duct.
b: Basilar membrane varies in stiffness from base (high‑freq) to apex (low‑freq)
Tectorial membrane overlies hair cells
Type IV collagen forms basement membranes of the organ of Corti

sections.p: Anteriorly the cochlea contacts the internal auditory canal; posteriorly it is adjacent to the vestibular aqueduct. The facial nerve runs in the facial canal just lateral to the cochlea.
b: Facial nerve (VII) runs in the fallopian canal
Cochlear nerve fibers join the vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII)

sections.p: The labyrinthine artery, a branch of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) or basilar artery, gives rise to the cochlear artery that supplies the stria vascularis and organ of Corti.
b: Cochlear artery supplies the stria vascularis
Ischemia causes sudden sensorineural loss

sections.p: Sensory innervation is via the cochlear branch of the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII). Hair cells release glutamate onto afferent fibers that ascend to the cochlear nucleus.
b: Inner hair cells: primary afferent transducers
Outer hair cells: amplify basilar‑membrane motion

sections.p: Sound waves cause the tympanic membrane to vibrate, generating pressure waves in the perilymph of the scala vestibuli. These travel through the helicotrema to the scala tympani, moving the basilar membrane and deflecting hair cell stereocilia against the tectorial membrane, producing neural impulses.
b: Base responds to high frequencies
Apex responds to low frequencies
Hair cells adapt to continuous sound (peripheral adaptation)

sections.p: Damage to the cochlear hair cells, stria vascularis, or auditory nerve leads to sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). Common causes include ototoxic drugs, infectious meningitis, sudden vascular occlusion, and trauma.
b: Ototoxicity: aminoglycosides, loop diuretics
Infectious: bacterial meningitis, TB meningitis
Vascular: AICA infarct
Trauma: temporal bone fracture

t.b: What type of hearing loss is present? Confirms sensorineural pattern and severity.
Is there a retro‑cochlear lesion or labyrinthine infarct? Detects tumors, infarcts, or inflammation.
Are infectious causes present? Guides antimicrobial therapy when imaging unavailable.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams: the cochlea’s base processes high‑frequency sounds; the organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane; blood supply is via the cochlear artery; sudden SNHL is a vascular emergency.
b: High‑freq → base, low‑freq → apex
Stria vascularis maintains endolymphatic potassium
Sudden SNHL → treat as emergency (steroids, rule out vascular cause)

whenToSeekHelp: Severe vertigo with hearing loss after head trauma
Progressive bilateral hearing loss in a child

faq.q: Why does damage to the base of the cochlea affect high‑frequency hearing?
faq.a: The basilar membrane is stiffest at the base, so high‑frequency vibrations peak there; loss of hair cells there removes high‑tone perception.

faq.q: Can hearing recover after ototoxic injury?
faq.a: If outer hair cells are damaged, recovery is unlikely; early cessation of the offending drug may prevent further loss.

faq.q: What is the role of Type IV collagen in the cochlea?
faq.a: It forms basement membranes that support the organ of Corti; defects can cause hereditary hearing loss.
